White-tailed tropicbird (Phaethon lepturus) is a pelagic seabird found throughout tropical oceans, and its life history is shaped by the energetic demands of oceanic foraging. Hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated for approximately 41 days [ab = approximately 41 days] at a mean nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that reflects the constraints of maintaining embryo development within a relatively thin-shelled egg in a hot, exposed crevice. Upon hatching, the altricial nestling weighs a mere 35 grams [Wwb = 35 grams], a modest starting mass that is typical for a bird that will undergo a pronounced growth trajectory to its adult size. This initial body mass, recorded from measurements of newly emerged chicks on stable nest sites, underscores the substantial provisioning effort required from both parents during the subsequent brooding phase.

The growth trajectory of the nestling culminates in the achievement of flight feathers and full independence from parental care. Fledging, or the first flight from the nest, occurs when the young bird is approximately 71 days [tx = approximately 71 days] old, a developmental milestone measured under the typical thermal conditions of the breeding colony at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This relatively short nestling period for a seabird of this body size is consistent with the species' strategy of exploiting ephemeral food resources in oligotrophic waters. The fledgling, now independent, must rapidly hone its foraging skills in the open ocean while continuing to build body mass toward the adult body mass of 410 grams [Wwi = 410 grams] that characterizes a fully grown individual.

Sexual maturation in the White-tailed tropicbird proceeds according to a schedule typical of tropical seabirds, with a distinct delay between fledging independence and the onset of reproductive activity. Under the ambient thermal conditions of the breeding colony, which often reach 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], puberty is typically attained at 213 days [tp = 213 days]. This age marks the onset of gonadal activity, yet most individuals do not breed immediately upon reaching this developmental threshold. The protracted period leading to sexual maturity, which is considerably longer than the time taken to achieve adult body size, suggests that young birds require an extended period to accumulate sufficient foraging experience and establish condition necessary for successful reproduction.

The species' reproductive schedule is highly constrained, reflecting the challenges of raising a single offspring in resource-poor environments. Following the attainment of puberty, first successful reproduction is typically deferred until approximately one year after birth. Under the thermal regime of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the age at first brood is recorded at 365 days [tR = 365 days]. This schedule results in a maximum reproductive rate characterized by a single egg per single clutch [N_R_i = single egg per single clutch], with intervals between successive breeding attempts extending to approximately ten months [F_R_i = approximately ten months]. This exceptionally low reproductive output is among the lowest recorded for any Pelecaniformes of its body mass.

Longevity records for this species, largely derived from data on the closely related Red-tailed tropicbird (Phaethon rubricauda), indicate an extraordinary potential lifespan under favorable conditions. With a documented maximum longevity of 11936 days [am = 11936 days] at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the White-tailed tropicbird belongs to a select group of seabirds capable of surviving for over three decades in the wild. This extended lifespan is critical for population persistence given the exceptionally low annual reproductive output of one egg per decade-long breeding cycle. The combination of delayed maturation, low fecundity, and high adult survival conforms to the classic slow life-history pace of tropical seabirds, a strategy that buffers populations against the stochasticity of oceanic food availability.
